To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

moderate alcohol intake was associated only with ER positive BC risk in women with low predicted familial BC risk and that current cigarette smoking was associated only with BC risk in women who also consume alcohol.

moderate alcohol intake was associated an increased risk of BC in women who had a low familial risk of developing BC, and that smoking was associated with increased risk of BC among women with high familial risk and who also consumed alcohol.
moderate alcohol consumption and current smoking were associated with increased risk of ER-positive, but not ER-negative BC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of alcohol intake and smoking on breast cancer (BC), particularly in relation to a woman's familial risk profile.
the role of alcohol consumption, cigarette smoke and familial BC risk.
understanding how alcohol and smoking interact to affect BC risk.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
moderate alcohol consumption and smoking may increase BC risk, particularly in women at low familial risk.
alcohol consumption is not associated with increased BC in women at high risk of familial BC but may be associated with increased risk in those at low familial risk.
the association of smoking with BC risk is unclear and the association of moderate alcohol consumption with BC is likely to be limited to women with ER positive disease and low familial risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
women with a low FRP who consume alcohol and are current smokers may be at the highest BC risk.
women with a lower predicted familial risk of BC should be encouraged to reduce their alcohol intake and women with higher predicted familial risk should be encouraged to stop smoking.
women who are at lower predicted risk of BC and who drink alcohol should be advised to reduce their alcohol intake.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the associations between smoking and alcohol and BC may differ by FRP.
the associations between smoking and drinking and BC risk are not uniform and may vary by ER status and FRP.
associations between alcohol consumption and cigarette smoking with BC risk are likely modified by a woman's FRP and ER status.
